content: Vasa previa is an obstetric complication characterized by fetal blood vessels crossing or running in close proximity to the internal cervical os. These vessels are located within the fetal membranes and are not supported by the umbilical cord or placental tissue, making them highly susceptible to rupture when the membranes rupture. The condition occurs when fetal blood vessels traverse the membranes over the internal cervical os. These vessels may originate from a velamentous insertion of the umbilical cord or may connect an accessory (succenturiate) placental lobe to the main placental disk. If these vessels rupture, the bleeding originates from the fetoplacental circulation, leading to rapid fetal exsanguination and, subsequently, fetal death. Vasa previa is more commonly associated with certain risk factors, including velamentous insertion of the umbilical cord, the presence of accessory placental lobes, and multiple gestations. The diagnosis of vasa previa is rarely confirmed before delivery. However, it may be suspected during antenatal ultrasound when color-flow Doppler imaging reveals a blood vessel crossing the membranes over the internal cervical os. Definitive diagnosis is typically made after delivery through examination of the placenta and fetal membranes. Treatment for vasa previa involves immediate intervention, usually in the form of an emergency cesarean delivery, to prevent fetal exsanguination and ensure the best possible outcome.
